🌍 AI in your world · Lesson 14 · 2 min read

How Apps Choose for You

How video, music and shopping apps decide what to show you next, which signals they read, and how to stay in charge of your feed.

Every feed is a guess

A video app has millions of videos, but your screen has room for a few. Something has to choose. That something is a recommendation system: a model that guesses, for each video, how likely you are to watch it, and shows the best guesses first. Your home page, your “For you” feed, the next song and “Customers also bought” are all made this way, for each person separately.

Did you know? In 2018, YouTube's product chief said that more than 70% of the time people spend watching YouTube comes from its recommendations, not from searching.

Two big ideas

The first idea is more of the same: you watched a cooking video, so here is another cooking video. The second is cleverer: people like you. The app finds people whose history looks like yours and shows you what they liked that you haven't seen yet. This is called collaborative filtering, and it works without knowing what a video is about. Real apps mix both ideas with many more signals.

What the app reads

Apps learn much more from what you do than from what you say. They notice how long you watch before you scroll, what you skip in two seconds, what you watch twice, share, search for, and even what time of day you watch. A long watch says “more of this” louder than a like. Each of these is a signal, and your feed changes with every one of them.

Did you know? Try it: watch a few videos on one new topic all the way through, and notice how quickly more of them appear in your feed.

Bubbles, and taking control

Because you can only watch what you're shown, and what you watch decides what you're shown, a feed can narrow into a filter bubble. Apps are also usually built to keep you watching, which isn't always what's best for you. You have more control than it seems: search for new topics, follow different people, tap “Not interested”, pause or clear your watch history, and turn off autoplay when you want to stop.

Did you know? Some apps let you see why something was recommended, or turn off the personalised feed. Look in the menu of a post (“Why am I seeing this?”) or in the app's settings.

Key points

  • A recommendation system guesses what you'll watch and shows its best guesses first, for each person separately.
  • Two big ideas: more of the same, and people like you (collaborative filtering).
  • Watching, skipping and searching are signals; a feed can narrow into a bubble, and you can widen it on purpose.

Check yourself

Your feed shows almost only football now, though you like other things too. What's the best way to widen it?

Show the answer

Right answer: Search for other topics, watch some, and tap “Not interested” on a few football videos

Your feed learns from what you do. Searching for and watching other topics gives it new signals, and “Not interested” tells it to show less of something. More football would make the bubble even tighter, and the app only knows what you've shown it.
